questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the Sinai covenant and show its centrality in the life of the Israelites.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Sinai (Horeb) covenant is the agreement concluded between God and the Israelites at Mount Sinai after the Exodus from Egypt, reported in Exodus 19-24 and renewed in Exodus 34. It is the foundation of Israel's identity as the people of God.

**1. The setting and the nature of the covenant.** God had delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt by grace. At Sinai he proposed a relationship: "if you will obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples... a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:5-6). The covenant begins with what God has done (liberation) and then states what the people must do (obedience); it is therefore a relationship before it is a law. The people answered, "All that the Lord has spoken we will do" (Exodus 19:8).

**2. Its content.** (i) The Ten Commandments (Exodus 20), covering duties toward God (one God, no images, the name of God, the Sabbath) and toward neighbour (parents, life, marriage, property, truth, desire). (ii) The "Book of the Covenant" (Exodus 21-23), with civil, social and religious laws. (iii) Instructions for the tabernacle and its worship (Exodus 25 onward).

**3. The ratification.** Moses read the book of the covenant, the people promised obedience, and the covenant was sealed with the sprinkling of the blood of sacrifices, followed by a meal in God's presence (Exodus 24).

**4. Its centrality in the life of the Israelites.**
(i) *Identity:* Israel saw itself as the people chosen by God, bound to him by covenant.
(ii) *Law and morality:* the commandments became the standard of right and wrong in family, justice and society.
(iii) *Worship:* the tabernacle, priesthood, Sabbath and festivals such as the Passover flow from the covenant.
(iv) *History and politics:* later kings, judges and the monarchy were judged by their loyalty to the covenant; Deuteronomy renews it before the entry into Canaan.
(v) *Prophecy:* the prophets accused Israel of breaking the covenant and called the people back to it; blessing and curse were understood in covenant terms.
(vi) *Hope:* after the exile, the people looked for a restored or "new" covenant (Jeremiah 31).

**5. Its fragility.** The golden calf (Exodus 32) showed that the covenant could be broken at once; God nevertheless renewed it (Exodus 34), which shows the primacy of his mercy.

**Conclusion.** The Sinai covenant made Israel a people under God's rule with a law, a worship and a mission. Almost every later feature of Old Testament religion can be traced back to it, which explains its central place in Israelite life.
